mcqs.chapter: Metabolic Disorders of Urea Cycle, Complex Mole...
mcqs.question: "Tomcat urine" is characteristically seen in ________
mcqs.explanation: Tomcat urine is characteristically seen in multiple carboxylase deficiency . It is named so because of its peculiar odour.277

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 28-year-old woman in labor comes to the emergency department at 37 weeks gestation . She never had a prenatal checkup . The routine screening revealed she is HIV -positive . Which of the following method is least likely to prevent the perinatal transmission of HIV ?

options.c: Administration of ART prophylaxis to baby after birth

mcqs.explanation: Vaginal cleansing before delivery is least likely to prevent the perinatal transmission of HIV . Methods to prevent perinatal transmission of HIV include the following : • Antiretroviral therapy (ART ): • Single -dose nevirapine at the onset of labor followed by a single dose to the newborn within 72 hours of birth. • Zidovudine can also be used from the 2nd trimester onwards throughout pregnancy and for 6 weeks after birth to infancy. • Breastfed infants should receive NVP for 6 weeks if the mother is receiving cART , or NVP for the duration of breastfeeding if the mother is not on therapy . Formula-fed infants in resource -limited countries should receive ZDV bid or NVP qd for 6 weeks . • Elective cesarean section * • Breastfeeding : Usually contraindicated , except in developing countries where breastfeeding may be continued for 6 months. *Note : Maternal cART is documented to decrease the rate of perinatal HIV -1 transmission to <2%, and <1% if the mother's viral RNA level is <1,000 copies /mL at delivery . Thus, elective C-section at 38 weeks of gestation should be considered only for women whose viral load is >1,000 copies / mL in late gestation , to further reduce the risk of vertical transmission. Guidelines for the use of antiretroviral drugs during C-section are as follows : • For elective (planned ) C-section , ART should be given prior to the operation. • Women on lifelong ART should continue their standard ART regimen. • In case of emergency C-section in pregnant women who are not on ART , the three -drug regimen should be started before the surgery and continued thereafter .291

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A worried couple brought their 4-day-old baby to the pediatrician due to difficulty in feeding and abnormal posture . The baby was delivered at home and the mother never had a prenatal checkup . On examination, the baby's body was rigid, with flexed upper limb and extended back. The umbilical cord was covered with cow dung. The mother says it's their tradition, and that the dirt helps with the falling off of the cord. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?

options.a: The toxin responsible affects the excitatory neurons
options.b: Metronidazole is given as a treatment
options.c: It occurs in infants of unimmunized mothers

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of neonatal tetanus . It is caused by a neurotoxin produced by Clostridium tetani, which inhibits inhibitory neurons, not excitatory neurons. Clostridium tetani is a spore -forming obligate anaerobe commonly found in soil, dust , and gastrointestinal tracts of various animals. The baby's umbilical stump covered with cow dung serves as the source of infection . It also occurs in infants of unimmunized mothers. Tetanus typically manifests within 3-12 days of birth as progressive difficulty in feeding , rigidity, or spasms. Tetanus toxin binds at the neuromuscular junction and enters the motor nerve; it is then transported to the alpha-motoneuron via retrograde axonal transport. Subsequently , the toxin enters the adjacent spinal inhibitory interneurons, where it prevents the release of the neurotransmitters glycine and \023-aminobutyric acid. This leads to blockade of normal antagonistic muscle inhibition, while agonist muscles undergo sustained contraction without relaxing. Neonatal tetanus presents with progressive feeding difficulty (sucking and swallowing ), irritability, and crying. Characteristic features include reduced movement or complete muscle paralysis, rigidity, and spasms. These features may or may not be associated with opisthotonos . Treatment includes supportive care in the form of muscle relaxants ( diazepam), along with the administration of human tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) and metronidazole , which is the antibiotic of choice . Parenteral penicillin G can serve as an alternate antibiotic. Excising the umbilical stump in a baby with neonatal tetanus is no longer recommended .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.chapter: Measles, Mumps, Rubella and Other Viral Infections
mcqs.question: You are a pediatrics resident posted in the labor room. You are examining a baby which was delivered via C-section a few minutes ago. You notice that the baby has zig-zag hypertrophic cutaneous scarring in a dermatomal distribution on the left side of the limbs and face . He also has a small head and small limbs. Antenatal history of the mother will be significant for which of the following infection ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of congenital varicella syndrome. Hence , antenatal history of varicella infection would be significant in the mother of this baby. Fetal varicella infection occurs if the mother gets infected during the first half of pregnancy. Clinical features include : • Cicatrix, a zigzag scarring in a dermatomal distribution • Microphthalmia • Cataracts • Optic atrophy • Chorioretinitis • Microcephaly • Limb hypoplasia • Motor and sensory deficits .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: An infant was brought to the paediatrician with complaints of vomiting and abdominal distention . The parents inform that the baby passes stools that look like currant jelly . On ultrasonography , a target sign was observed. Which of the following is not true about this condition?

options.a: Rota virus vaccine is not associated with increased risk
options.c: The most common cause is idiopathic
options.d: The most common location is ileocolic region

mcqs.explanation: The clinical vignette is suggestive of intussusception and the rotavirus vaccine is associated with an increased risk , albeit only a slightly increased risk Intussusception occurs when a portion of the alimentary tract is telescoped into an adjacent segment . The most common location of intussusception is ileocolic . Ileoileal location is seen postoperatively and in Henoch–Sch\366nlein Purpura. 90% of cases of intussusception in children are idiopathic in nature. It can be seen in infants during the weaning period following the introduction of new food, vaccination , or upper respiratory tract infection . The currently approved rotavirus vaccines are associated with a slightly increased risk of intussusception . Lead points are more common in children older than 2 years of age and can cause recurrent intussusception. Some recognizable lead points are as follows : enlarged submucosal Peyer's patch, Meckel 's diverticulum, intestinal polyp , neurofibroma, intestinal duplication cysts , leiomyomas , hamartomas, anastomotic suture line, enterostomy tube , hemangioma, or malignant conditions such as lymphoma or Kaposi sarcoma.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: The intestinal biopsy report of a 7-year-old boy evaluated for chronic watery diarrhoea revealed a flat intestinal mucosa. Which of the following conditions would you suspect in this child?
mcqs.explanation: Chronic diarrhoea with a flat intestinal mucosa can be seen in conditions Tropical sprue , giardiasis, and HIV enteropathy . Causes of the flat intestinal mucosa (subtotal or total villous atrophy): • Celiac disease • Tropical sprue • Giardiasis • Bacterial overgrowth • HIV enteropathy • Eosinophilic gastroenteritis • Cow's milk or soy protein enteropathy • Graft versus host disease • Chemo or radiotherapy • Protein-energy malnutrition • Tuberculosis or lymphoma Amoebiasis and neutrophilic gastroenteritis may also rarely have villous atrophy but the presentation is generally acute . Amoebiasis is characteristically associated with dysentery and biopsy would reveal a flask-shaped ulcer.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs are not used in the treatment of hepatitis B?
mcqs.explanation: Ribavirin is a drug used in the treatment of hepatitis C, not hepatitis B. Indications for starting antiviral therapy in chronic hepatitis B are: • Patients without cirrhosis • HBeAg + with HBV DNA >20,000 IU/mL and ALT level >2 times the upper limit of normal • HBeAg -ve with HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL and ALT level >2 times the upper limit of normal • Patients with compensated cirrhosis and an HBV DNA >2000 IU/mL • Patients developing acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis. Drugs used in the treatment of hepatitis B are: • First-line treatment : Entecavir or tenofovir • Other drugs: • Pegylated interferon-alpha • Telbivudine • Lamivudine • Adefovir

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A preterm infant in the NICU was observed to have marked nasal flare, distinct xiphoid retractions, minimal intercostal retractions, and inspiratory lag with an audible grunt. What would be the Silverman Anderson score?
mcqs.explanation: The Silverman -Anderson score of the child would be 8. Calculation of the Silverman -Anderson score of this child: Total score: A score of more than 7 indicates respiratory failure. The Silverman -Anderson score is a commonly used score to assess respiratory distress . It helps to assess the progression of distress over time and initiate treatment . It is more suited for preterms with respiratory distress syndrome. Scoring is to be done every half an hour and charting is carried out to monitor progress . mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: 10 -month-old Ishaan was presented to the OPD with a 3-day history of lower respiratory tract symptoms and an expiratory wheeze . Chest X-ray showed mild peribronchial thickening. Which of the following statements is false regarding the condition described ?

options.a: The risk is higher for infants with young mothers or mothers who smoked during pregnancy.
options.b: It is more common in children who have not been breastfed .
options.c: The mainstay of treatment is antibiotics.
options.d: There is a higher incidence of wheezing and asthma in children with a history of bronchiolitis.

mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute bronchiolitis. The treatment is mainly supportive . Hypoxemic children should receive cool, humidified oxygen . Rarely, a child might develop respiratory failure and require hospitalization and invasive ventilation.436 It is more common in boys, in those who have not been breastfed , and in those who live in crowded conditions. The risk is higher for infants with young mothers or mothers who smoked during pregnancy. Acute bronchiolitis is predominantly a viral disease caused by respiratory syncytial virus (RSV ) and antibiotics are not indicated . There is a higher incidence of wheezing and asthma in children with a history of bronchiolitis.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: All the following are true about Macleod syndrome except that _______.

options.a: It is also called Swyer -James syndrome.
options.b: It is not a true emphysema .
options.c: It is mostly linked to adenovirus.
options.d: Affected lung is larger in size compared to unaffected lung.

mcqs.explanation: Macleod syndrome refers to the inability of the lungs to grow after a severe obstructive bronchiolitis. Children with this condition often have chronic cough , recurrent pneumonia, and wheezing . On CT scan, the affected lung shows small size and decreased vascularity, hyperexpansion , and hyperlucency (false emphysema ). It is also called Swyer –James syndrome. It is mostly linked to adenovirus. Patients respond well to bronchodilators.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A good surgeon knows when not to operate . As a pediatric surgeon , on which of the following cases of VSD would you operate ?
mcqs.explanation: Severe pulmonary vascular disease unresponsive to pulmonary vasodilators is a contraindication to the closure of a VSD - due to permanent remodeling of the pulmonary vasculature.469 Indications for surgical closure of a VSD include : • Patients at any age with large defects in whom clinical symptoms and failure to thrive cannot be controlled medically ; • Infants between 6 and 12 mo of age with moderate to large defects associated with pulmonary hypertension, even if the symptoms are controlled by medication; and patients older than 24 mo with a Qp: Qs ratio greater than 2: 1. • Patients with a supracristal VSD of any size are usually referred for surgery because of their higher risk for developing aortic valve regurgitation A child with large VSD showing transient improvement in symptoms with better exercise tolerance may be the first sign of developing pulmonary hypertension and indicates an urgent need for evaluation and immediate surgery - the increased pulmonary pressure reduces the amount of blood pushed into the lungs and thereby , congestion transiently. The presence of a mid-diastolic , low-pitched rumble at the apex is caused by increased blood flow across the mitral valve and usually indicates a Qp: Qs ratio \034of 2: 1. This murmur is best appreciated with the bell of the stethoscope . Surgical risks are somewhat higher for defects in the muscular septum , particularly apical defects and multiple (Swiss cheese –type ) VSDs. These patients may require pulmonary arterial banding if symptomatic , with subsequent de -banding and repair of multiple VSDs at an older age .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A primary school teacher notices a peculiar behavior in one of her pupils . Whenever he plays with his friends, she notices that her fingers and lips turn blue . The child then squats for sometime after which he feels better . Which of the following does not occur during squatting?

options.a: It increases the systemic vascular resistance
options.b: It increases the magnitude of right-to-left shunt
options.c: Leads to trapping of deoxygenated blood in lower limbs

mcqs.explanation: Squatting decreases the magnitude of the right-to-left shunt in a child with tetralogy of Fallot (TOF) .490 The child feels comfortable while squatting due to two compensatory mechanisms: • Increasing systemic vascular resistance and, thus , decreasing the magnitude of the right-to-left shunt across the ventricular septal defect (VSD). Therefore, more blood goes to the lungs for oxygenation . • Trapping deoxygenated venous blood in the lower limbs.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A pediatrician suspects vesicoureteric reflux in a girl with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections . What is the investigation of choice to confirm this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) is the investigation of choice for vesicoureteral reflux. Recurrent febrile urinary tract infections in a child should raise the suspicion of an anatomical defect like vesicoureteric reflux as the cause . Compared to other investigations, a VCUG provides more anatomic information. It can demonstrate :531 • Vesicoureteral reflux • Duplex collecting system • Ectopic ureter • Paraureteral (bladder ) diverticulum • Bladder outlet obstruction • Signs of voiding dysfunction , such as a spinning top urethra

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the most common cause of ventriculomegaly in newborns?
mcqs.explanation: Aqueductal stenosis is the most common cause of ventriculomegaly and hydrocephalus in newborns. Ventriculomegaly is the dilation of the ventricles. When ventriculomegaly occurs in association with raised cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pressure , it is called hydrocephalus . Pathologic etiologies can be congenital or acquired. Congenital causes include structural abnormalities such as aqueductal stenosis , agenesis of the corpus callosum, Dandy-Walker malformations, Chiari malformations, and neural tube defects . Acquired causes are intracranial infections (cytomegalovirus , toxoplasmosis), intracranial hemorrhage, ischemic injury, and brain parenchymal tumors. Aqueductal stenosis is the narrowing or obstruction of the cerebral aqueduct , a narrow channel that connects the third and fourth ventricles in the brain . As a result , the fluid accumulates within the ventricles, causing them to enlarge . Treatment for aqueductal stenosis includes ventriculostomy , diuretics , serial lumbar punctures in specific cases , and CSF diversion. In severe cases , CSF diversion procedures (shunting), may be necessary to redirect the flow of CSF and relieve pressure on the brain .555

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A newborn presented with high-grade fever, poor feeding and incessant cry for the last 2 days. Multiple episodes of vomiting are present as well . On examination, hypotonia is present along with weak reflexes . The patient is admitted and during rounds, subtle lip-smacking seizures are also observed along with a vacant stare. CSF examination shows reduced glucose , increased protein, and increased leukocytes with predominant neutrophils . Which of the following organism is unlikely to cause this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The acute features of fever, poor feeding, incessant cry, vomiting and seizures points toward a likely diagnosis of neonatal meningitis. The CSF findings correlate with that of bacterial meningitis due to purulent appearance , increased proteins , decreased glucose and a predominance of polymorphs . Neonatal meningitis is not caused by Neisseria meningitidis because , in neonates , bacteria are often acquired from the maternal vaginal flora. The common causes of acute bacterial meningitis:Age group Organism Neonates Group B streptococci ,Escheri chia coli,Listeria574 Age group Organism Infants and children Neisseria meningitidis ,Strept ococcus pneumoniae ,andHae mophilus influenzae Adolescents and young adult s S.pneumoniae ,N.meningitidi s

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Ayesha is a 9th standard girl who presented with a neck swelling , which began more than a year ago. Her mother says she is embarrassed about it and always covers her neck with a shawl when she goes to school. Her menstrual cycles have also become irregular as of late . Blood tests reveal slightly elevated TSH levels and the presence of thyroid peroxidase antibodies . Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: The presence of thyroid peroxidase antibodies (TPO-Abs) and elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level in a child with a goitre is suggestive of chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis . Chronic lymphocytic (Hashimoto) thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease . Clinical presentation can include goitre, growth retardation, and other features of hypothyroidism . The thyroid is diffusely enlarged , firm, and non-tender.591 TSH is moderately elevated and TPO-Abs and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (anti-Tg Abs) can be detected . The image given below shows goitre due to Hashimoto's thyroiditis .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 4-year-old boy was brought by his mother with new-onset nocturnal bedwetting . She also reported , he has been drinking more water for the last 3-4 months. 24-hour urine volume was 4 liters and the urine osmolality was low. ADH assays recorded a value was 0.7 pg /mL . T1 weighted MRI brain indicated an absence of a pituitary bright spot . What is the treatment of choice for his condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of central diabetes insipidus . The treatment of choice is desmopressin. It is a vasopressin analog (V2 receptor agonist). It can be administered intranasally, or subcutaneously . Option A: Leuprolide is a GnRH (gonadotropin-releasing hormone) analog used in the treatment of prostate cancer, breast cancer, and endometriosis . Option B: Thiazides paradoxically exert an antidiuretic effect in DI but are not the drug of choice . They are generally used in nephrogenic DI.625 Option D: Terlipressin is a long-acting analog on vasopressin that acts on V1 receptors of vascular smooth muscle . It is used as a vasopressor in shock and acute variceal bleeding .

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Cancer-'The emperor of all maladies spares no one'. Which of the following is the most common childhood malignancy?
mcqs.explanation: Leukemias are the most common childhood malignancies. Among these , acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL ) is the most common, accounting for about 77 % of childhood leukemias . Most commons in childhood malignancies: • Second most common malignancy in childhood : Brain tumor • Third most common malignancy in children: Lymphoma • Most common solid tumor in children: Brain tumor

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A 6-year-old boy is brought with complaints of abdominal distension , fatigue , and night sweats for the past 4 months. He also has a 2-month history of postprandial fullness and recurrent non-bilious vomiting. On examination, he is pale , has hepatosplenomegaly and shifting dullness . A CT scan shows mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymph node enlargement . A biopsy specimen of the mesenteric lymph node reveals tumor cells with high mitotic index and starry sky pattern. The cytogenetic study revealed t(8;14).To stage the disease , which of the following systems would you use ?
mcqs.explanation: Retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymphadenopathy with hepatosplenomegaly , anemia, and short duration of disease , point towards a diagnosis of lymphoid neoplasms .The classic translocation of t(8;14) and starry sky appearance with a high mitotic index on HPE point toward a diagnosis of Burkitt lymphoma. Burkitt's lymphoma is the most common type of Non-Hodgkin lymphoma worldwide . St Jude system of staging is used for staging childhood non-Hodgkin lymphoma. The current revised staging system used for NHL is the International Pediatric Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma Staging System (IPNHLSS) which reflects our increasing ability to diagnose lower levels of organ involvement with disease. For instance, the older staging system (St. Jude/Murphy classification ) did not account for molecular or flow cytometry involvement of bone marrow , which is now reflected in the new system.Disease System of staging Hodgkin lymphoma Ann–Arbor staging Non-Hodgkin Lymphom a St Jude(Murphy ) stagin g Chronic lymphoid leuke mia Rai stagingBinet staging

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: What is the most common intraocular tumor diagnosed in the pediatric age group?
mcqs.explanation: 685 Retinoblastoma is the most common intraocular tumor of the pediatric age group. It is an embryonal malignancy of the retina.

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: Pinky , a small child with Kawasaki disease is admitted to the ward for treatment . Which of the following feature would you not expect to see in her?
mcqs.explanation: Purulent conjunctivitis is not a feature of Kawasaki disease . Bilateral nonexudative conjunctival infection with limbal sparing is characteristically seen in Kawasaki disease . Kawasaki disease is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome and is commonly seen in children between 3 months to 5 years of age .716

mcqs.subject: Pediatrics
mcqs.question: A pediatric resident administers 0.5-1 mg of phytonadione intramuscularly to all newborn infants in the ward. Deficiency of which of the following factors is prevented by this medication?
mcqs.explanation: 731 Intramuscular injection of 0.5-1 mg of phytonadione is given to all newborn infants because it prevents the deficiency of factor VII that occurs transiently after birth. Hemorrhagic disease of the newborn is caused by a transient deficiency of vitamin K–dependent factors, factors II , VII , IX, and X. Causes include : • Lack of free vitamin K from the mother • Absence of the bacterial intestinal flora normally responsible for the synthesis of vitamin K. It is responsive to and prevented by vitamin K therapy (0.5-1 mg of phytonadione ).

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following hormones act through the receptor shown in the image below ?
mcqs.explanation: The receptor in the given image uses tyrosine kinase signaling. Insulin acts through this receptor to exert its functions. Other hormones acting via tyrosine kinase signaling: • Growth hormone • Growth factors like VEGF, PDGF, FGF, NGF • Prolactin • Leptin

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding the dose -response curve shown in the image below ?

options.b: C is more potent than A
options.c: B is more potent than A

mcqs.explanation: In the above image, drug B is a competitive antagonist. In competitive antagonism, the DRC is shifted to the right whereas in non-competitive antagonism the DRC is flattened . Thus in the above image Drug B is the Competitive antagonist while drug C is the non-competitive antagonist. Potency : • It is defined as the amount of drug needed to produce a given response . • A highly potent drug evokes a given response at low concentrations and vice-versa. • The more the curve is on the left in a dose -response curve (DRC), the greater is its potency . • Thus, in the above image, the potency is drug A > drug C > drug B. Efficacy : • It is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug.42 • It expresses the effect produced by the receptors when bound by a certain drug. • In the log dose -response curve, the perpendicular height represents the drug efficacy . • Thus, in the above image, the efficacy is drug A = drug B > drug C.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: What type of antagonism is shown by drugs A and B in the following dose -response curve?
mcqs.explanation: The parallel rightward shift of the agonist dose -response curve (DRC) is seen with competitive antagonism. Increasing the dose of the agonist can result in the same maximal response . In non-competitive antagonism, there will be flattening of the agonist DRC.43

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: The graph below shows the relationship between the log(dose ) and the response of three drugs, A, B, and C. Which of these drugs has the highest potency ?
mcqs.explanation: Drug A has the highest potency . Potency : • It is defined as the amount of drug needed to produce a given response . A highly potent drug evokes a given response at low concentrations and vice-versa. • The more the curve is on the left in a dose -response curve (DRC), the greater is its potency . • Thus, in the above image, the potency is Drug A >Drug B> Drug C. Efficacy : • It is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug. It reflects the capacity of the drug to activate a receptor and produce the response . • In the log dose -response curve, the perpendicular height represents the drug efficacy . • Thus, in the above image, the efficacy is Drug A = Drug B > Drug C. • Drugs having a similar pharmacological effect can have different efficacies e.g furosemide and metolazone are both diuretics but furosemide has greater efficacy than metolazone .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about the given dose -response curve?

options.a: Drug B is the most potent .
options.b: Drug B is the most efficacious .
options.c: Drug C is more efficacious than drug D.
options.d: Drug A is more potent than drug B.

mcqs.explanation: The more the curve is on the left in a dose -response curve (DRC), the greater is its potency . Hence , Drug B is the most potent . Potency : • It is defined as the amount of drug needed to produce a given response . • A highly potent drug evokes a given response at low concentrations and vice-versa.44 • In the above image, the potency is Drug B> Drug A > Drug C > Drug D. Efficacy : • It is defined as the maximum effect produced by the drug. It reflects the capacity of the drug to activate a receptor and produce the response . • In the log dose -response curve, the perpendicular height represents the drug efficacy . • Thus, in the above image, the efficacy is Drug A = Drug C =Drug D > Drug B. • Drugs having a similar pharmacological effect can have different efficacies e.g furosemide and metolazone are both diuretics but furosemide has greater efficacy than metolazone .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: What does the area between the dotted lines in this graph indicate ?
mcqs.explanation: The area between the dotted lines in the graph shows the therapeutic window . It is the range of steady -state concentrations of a drug that provides therapeutic efficacy with minimal toxicity . The therapeutic index (TI) describes a relationship between the doses of a drug that causes lethal or toxic effects with the dose that causes therapeutic effects . It is also called the therapeutic ratio. Mathematically , you can calculate TI by following way: Therapeutic Index = LD50/ED50 (or) Therapeutic Index = TD50/ED50 Where, • LD50 (Median Lethal dose ) is the minimum amount of drug that causes adverse effects in 50% of the population . LD50 could also be replaced with Toxic dose (TD50). • ED50 (Median Effective dose ) is the quantity of a drug that can produce desired therapeutic effects in 50% of the population .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Calculate the therapeutic index of a drug whose dose -response curves are plotted as shown below :
mcqs.explanation: The therapeutic index is 4. In the above graph, Median lethal dose (LD50) = 400 Median effective dose (ED50) = 10049 Therapeutic index (TI) = LD50/ED50. Hence , Therapeutic index (TI ) = 400 /100 = 4 Clinically, the therapeutic range bound by the dose that produces the minimal therapeutic effect and the dose that produces the maximal acceptable adverse effect is more relevant.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs if taken during pregnancy can lead to this adverse effect ?
mcqs.explanation: The baby has features suggestive of phocomelia and it results due to the consumption of thalidomide during pregnancy. Phocomelia is associated with underdeveloped limbs and absent pelvic bones. Both upper and lower limbs are affected and a part of the limbs may be missing. Fused fingers and missing thumbs are also seen . Thalidomide was originally used for the treatment of pregnancy-associated morning sickness but was withdrawn due to this adverse effect . It re-entered the market for the treatment of erythema nodosum leprosum . It also has antiangiogenic and immunomodulatory effects .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: The following table gives BP values before and after administration of drug 'X'. What would be the probable mechanism of action of drug 'X'?
mcqs.explanation: The probable mechanism of action of drug 'X' is \0351 and \0352 agonism. According to the given table , systolic BP and heart rate is increased due to \0351 agonistic effect , and diastolic BP is decreased by vasodilatation due to \0352 action. Option A: Action on �o 1 causes \032 DBP Option B: Action on M2 causes \031 HR and action on M3 causes vasodilatation and reflex increase in HR. Hence there is no net effect on heart rate Option C: �o 1 antagonism causes vasodilatation and \031 DBP. \0352 action causes vasodilatation and DBP \031

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: What is the scientific name of this plant whose roots & leaves were historically used in the treatment of asthma?
mcqs.explanation: The above plant is Datura stramonium, also called Jamestown or Jimsonweed . The active ingredient in Datura stramonium includes anticholinergic alkaloids such as atropine, scopolamine , and hyoscyamine . These were helpful in relieving the symptoms associated with asthma via inhibition of M3 receptors on bronchi, leading to a decrease in bronchospasm and tracheobronchial secretions .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient who is on treatment for glaucoma presented with the following finding during his routine follow -up. Which of the following drugs can cause this adverse effect ?
mcqs.explanation: The patient has presented with lid retraction which is most likely caused by the use of apraclonidine. It is a congener of clonidine that has primary �o 2 agonist action and a subsidiary �o 1 agonist action. Adverse effects like mydriasis and lid retraction are common with apraclonidine.155 Brimonidine is also a congener of clonidine with more �o 2 selectivity . Mydriasis and lid retraction are uncommon with this agent . Timolol and latanoprost do not cause lid retraction.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: The ophthalmologic examination of a patient who is on anti-glaucoma drugs shows the following finding. Identify the drug that might have resulted in this adverse effect .
mcqs.explanation: The ophthalmological examination shows a pearly white opacity of the lens suggestive of cataract. Anticholinesterase agents like echothiophate and cholinergic agonists like pilocarpine are known to be associated with cataract formation.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient who is on anti-glaucoma therapy presents with corneal findings as shown in the image below . This finding is most commonly observed with which of the following drugs?
mcqs.explanation: The bilateral whorl-like pattern of cream-colored lines on the cornea seen in the image is called cornea verticillata or vortex keratopathy. It is observed with the use of netarsudil . It is usually mild and reversible and not associated with any significant visual abnormalities. Netarsudil is approved for lowering intraocular pressure in patients with open -angle glaucoma or ocular hypertension . Other causes of corneal verticillata are: • Fabry's disease • Amiodarone • Chloroquine • Hydroxychloroquine • Indomethacin • Phenothiazines.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Choose the correct pair matching with the diagram:

options.a: A: Loop diuretics , B: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors
options.d: A: Thiazides, B: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors

mcqs.explanation: A is the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle and loop diuretics act on this part of the nephron. B is the distal convoluted tubule and thiazides act on this part of the nephron. Site of action of other diuretics : • Proximal tubule - carbonic anhydrase inhibitors • Collecting ducts and late distal tubule - epithelial sodium channel (ENaC) inhibitors and aldosterone antagonists

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient presented to the ER with dizziness and palpitations . ECG is shown below . Which of the following drugs cannot be used in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The scenario and ECG findings (absent P waves and RR intervals that are irregularly irregular) are suggestive of atrial fibrillation. Lignocaine is not used in atrial arrhythmias. Lignocaine is a class 1B anti-arrhythmic agent . It blocks Na+ channels mostly in the closed /inactivated state . It is not used in atrial arrhythmias because the atrial action potential is so short that the Na+ channels are in a closed / inactivated state for only a brief amount of time. Lignocaine is used in the acute treatment of ventricular tachycardia and ventricular fibrillation. Drugs mostly used for supraventricular arrhythmia are: • Adenosine • Verapamil • Diltiazem • Digoxin Drugs used for ventricular arrhythmia are: • Lidocaine • Mexiletine Drugs used in both conditions are: • Amiodarone • Beta-blockers • Class 1a / 1c antiarrhythmics

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Fundoscopic evaluation in an HIV patient showed CMV retinitis. He was started on intravenous foscarnet, a highly ionized drug. Which of the following statements is true about the drug?

options.b: Can cross the blood brain barrier easily

mcqs.explanation: Highly ionized drugs like foscarnet are mainly excreted by the kidneys. They are not reabsorbed from the renal tubules and are hence excreted unchanged by glomerular filtration. Dose reduction is necessary in renal impairment to avoid the accumulation of the drug and associated toxicity . The non-ionized forms of weak acids and bases undergo tubular reabsorption. Option B: The blood-brain barrier limits the entry of ionized, non-lipid soluble drugs. Option C: A drug is more readily absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract when it is in its unionized, more lipophilic form. Option D: As the ionized form has low lipid solubility , it cannot penetrate cell membranes easily .13

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient with congestive heart failure is being treated with an intravenous infusion of nesiritide. Which of the following receptors does this drug act through?
mcqs.explanation: Nesiritide is recombinant B-type natriuretic peptide . Natriuretic peptide receptors are transmembrane ligand-gated guanylyl cyclase receptors . Natriuretic peptides : • Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP): released from atrial storage granules in response to an increase in intravascular volume. It decreases blood pressure . • Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP): released from ventricular tissue in response to volume overload. Along with a decrease in blood pressure, it is known to reduce cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis. • C- type natriuretic peptide (CNP): synthesized in the brain and endothelial tissues and functions to stimulate long bone growth . ANP and BNP act on the NPR-A receptor . CNP acts on the NPR-B receptor .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A first-year resident administers an intramuscular injection to a patient by the Z track technique. What is the advantage of this technique ?
mcqs.explanation: The advantage of the 'Z-track technique ' for intramuscular administration is that it prevents skin staining. Z-track technique procedure : • Stretch the skin by pulling it laterally away from the intended point of injection. • Insert the needle into the site at a 90\037 angle, aspirate by pulling back to see if the needle has a penetrated vessel . • If blood is aspirated withdraw the needle , and repeat the procedure at another site with new equipment and medication. • If no blood is aspirated administer the injection. • Wait for 10 seconds and then withdraw the needle , and release the skin allowing the displaced tissue to seal the needle track. Advantages:64 • The 'Z-track' prevents leakage of the medication into the subcutaneous tissue and skin staining through the tract to the surface of the skin • Pain intensity is also reduced

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A young man is brought to the ER with a history of ingestion of carbamate-based insecticide . He is agitated with excessive sweating , lacrimation, and salivation. Which of the following should not be used for treatment ?
mcqs.explanation: Pralidoxime may be hazardous in oral poisoning with carbamate insecticides . It is not effective in carbamate anti-ChE poisoning as the anionic site required for attachment of oximes is occupied .90 Oximes are usually contraindicated in carbamate poisoning, as they do not reactivate the enzyme. They also have anti-ChE activity of their own that may worsen the condition. Option B: Atropine is the mainstay in the management of carbamate poisoning. Options C and D: Magnesium sulfate purgative and gastric lavage with activated charcoal can be tried in oral carbamate poisoning.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A delirious child was rushed to the ER with a history of ingestion of an unknown plant. On examination , his pulse rate was 150 beats per minute, and his skin was warm and dry. Pupils were dilated and bowel sounds were sluggish . Which of the following toxidromes is likely to be responsible for the symptoms in this child?
mcqs.explanation: 121 Mydriasis, tachycardia, dry mouth, atropine fever (warm, hot skin) and delirium are classical symptoms of anticholinergic overdose following the ingestion of plants that contain belladonna alkaloids. Physostigmine is the drug of choice for the treatment of atropine and belladonna poisoning.Option B: Sympathomimetics can cause mydriasis and tachycardia. Hyperthermia can be seen secondary to increased agitation and aggressive movements. However, delirium is rare and bowel sounds would be normal or increased in sympathomimetic toxidromes. Option C: Opioid overdose results in decreased bowel sounds but other symptoms are not seen . Option D: In sedative -hypnotic toxidrome, CNS depression and reduced bowel sounds are seen . But it does not cause tachycardia or change in pupil diameter .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs should not be given in a patient prone to developing angle -closure glaucoma?
mcqs.explanation: Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic having significant anticholinergic action. Drugs having significant anticholinergic action should be avoided or used with extreme caution in patients prone to developing acute angle-closure glaucoma. The anticholinergic action results in the relaxation of the sphincter pupillae muscle . This results in the iris coming in contact with the lens and thereby obstructing the movement of the aqueous from the posterior to the anterior chamber. This results in bulging of the iris and further leads to the obliteration of the narrow iridocorneal angle . This blocks the outflow of aqueous precipitating an acute attack of glaucoma.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient is to be started on digoxin therapy for heart failure. Despite already being on another drug, dose adjustment of digoxin is not necessary for this patient . Identify this drug.
mcqs.explanation: Levosimendan does not increase digitalis toxicity and hence would not require dose adjustment of digoxin. It is a combined Ca2+ channel sensitizer (troponin C binding) and PDE3 inhibitor.179 Digoxin is metabolized by P-glycoprotein and drugs that inhibit it increase the plasma levels of digoxin and may result in toxicity . The drugs that increase digoxin toxicity are: • Amiodarone • Quinidine • Propafenone • Verapamil • Captopril • Erythromycin • Gentamycin • Ranolazine

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following drugs reduces blood pressure primarily by directly decreasing the heart rate?
mcqs.explanation: Propranolol reduces blood pressure by directly decreasing the heart rate. It is a nonselective beta-blocker and blocks the beta 1 receptor of the heart (SA node) thus reducing the heart rate and blood pressure . It also reduces renin secretion by blocking beta 1 receptors in JG cells . Reduction in renin release also contributes to blood pressure reduction . Option B: Prazosin is a selective alpha 1 blocker and dilates both arteries and veins and may cause reflex tachycardia.198 Option C: Alpha methyldopa is a selective alpha 2 receptor agonist. Alpha 2 receptors are autoreceptors present on the presynaptic membrane. On stimulation, central sympathetic discharge is reduced . Alpha methyldopa can indirectly reduce heart rate. Option D: Nitroprusside is a vasodilator and may cause reflex tachycardia.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A 35-year-old man with asthma presents with complaints of increased urination. The doctor checks that he has been taking theophylline and counsels that it could be a side effect . What is the mechanism of action causing diuresis ?
mcqs.explanation: The diuretic effect of theophylline is due to the blockade of adenosine (A1) receptors . Theophylline is a methylxanthine drug that acts by - • Inhibition of phosphodiesterase enzyme (PDE) • PDE3 inhibition - relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle • PDE4 inhibition - inhibition cytokines and chemokine release , which leads to a decrease in immune cell migration and activation • Blockade of adenosine receptors inhibits bronchoconstriction, however, blockade of A1 receptors in the glomerular afferent arteriole and PCT causes diuresis . • Activating enzyme histone deacetylase-2, which is responsible for its anti-inflammatory action215

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia has mipomersen as part of his treatment regimen. By which of the following mechanisms does this drug act?
mcqs.explanation: Mipomersen is an antisense oligonucleotide that acts as an inhibitor of apo B-100 synthesis . Mipomersen binds to the mRNA of apo B-100 resulting in degradation of apo B-100 mRNA and eventually reduction of apo B-100 synthesis .242

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Your senior resident asks you to prescribe an orexin receptor inhibitor to a patient with insomnia. Which of the following drugs would you prescribe ?
mcqs.explanation: Suvorexant is an inhibitor of both orexin1 and orexin2 receptors . It is approved for the treatment of insomnia. Orexins are produced in the lateral hypothalamus neurons and play a major role in maintaining the sleep cycle . Orexins promote wakefulness , while antagonists at orexin receptors enhance REM and non-REM sleep . Option B: Doxepin is a tricyclic antidepressant and has H1 receptor antagonism effect . It is used for insomnia at lower doses . Option C: Ritanserin is a 5HT2A /2C receptor antagonist indicated in insomnia. Option D: Agomelatine is a melatonin receptor agonist and a 5HT2C receptor antagonist indicated in insomnia.267

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A known epileptic patient on levetiracetam has been seizure -free for 2 years. But he develops agitation and anger issues interfering with his day-to-day activities as a result of the drug intake. Which of the following measures is to be taken next?

options.a: Slowly taper the drug over next 6 months
options.b: Continue levetriacetam since a 5 year seizure free interval is needed
options.c: Stop levetiracetam and start on a different anti-epileptic
options.d: Discontinue the drug as he is seizure free

mcqs.explanation: The mood changes observed in the above patient must be due to an adverse effect of levetiracetam . Abrupt stoppage of the drug can result in rebound seizures . So the best management will be to slowly taper the drug over the next 6 months. Adverse effects of levetiracetam : • Somnolence • Asthenia • Ataxia • Dizziness. • Mood and behavioral changes • Psychotic reactions (rare)295

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following effects of chlorpromazine is not due to its antidopaminergic activity?
mcqs.explanation: Orthostatic hypotension is due to the alpha-receptor blocking the action of chlorpromazine. Chlorpromazine is a typical or first-generation antipsychotic with D2 blocking and additional alpha-receptor-blocking and anticholinergic activity. Option A: Dopamine inhibits prolactin release causing hypoprolactinemia and hence antidopaminergic action of chlorpromazine causes hyperprolactinemia . Option B: Extrapyramidal side effects occur due to D2 antagonism in the nigrostriatal region. Option C: The antiemetic action is due to D2 antagonism in the chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ ).314

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following dopamine agonists is an ergot derivative?
mcqs.explanation: Bromocriptine and pergolide are ergot derivatives that act as potent agonists at the D2 receptor . Pramipexole and ropinirole are non-ergot derivatives having D2/D3 receptor agonistic action. They are better tolerated and have fewer GI symptoms than bromocriptine.337 Dopamine agonists can be classified as follows : • Ergot derivatives - Bromocriptine, pergolide , cabergoline • Non-ergot derivatives - Pramipexole, ropinirole, apomorphine, rotigotine Dopaminergic agonists exert subtype -selective activation of dopaminergic receptors involved in the Parkinsonism circuit of the striatum.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: In children and adolescents treated with an SSRI , there appears to be an increased risk of particular ideations . Clinicians are therefore advised to remain vigilant of which of the following ?
mcqs.explanation: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs ) should be used carefully in the young for the management of depression due to increased suicidal ideation . In children and adolescents , there appears to be a slightly increased risk of suicidal ideations and attempts , but not of completed suicide . Somatic symptoms of depression improve faster than psychological symptoms when a patient is started on SSRIs and hence patients have the energy to act on their thoughts of deliberate self -harm and suicide (paradoxical suicide ).358

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Upon recovering from anesthesia , a patient started feeling cold accompanied by shivering. Which is the opioid indicated to treat this condition?
mcqs.explanation: Meperidine is commonly indicated for post -anesthetic shivering. It prevents post -anesthetic shivering by lowering the temperature threshold at which shivering is triggered by the hypothalamus . A single dose of 12 .5 to 35mg meperidine (pethidine ) is effective in the treatment of postanesthetic shivering. Infusion-related chills and rigors associated with amphotericin B, aldesleukin , trastuzumab, and alemtuzumab are also managed with meperidine in combination with other agents .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A 40-year-old man with alcohol dependence is referred to a rehabilitation center for deaddiction . Which of the following drugs would you not prescribe for maintenance of deaddiction ?
mcqs.explanation: Morphine, an opioid receptor agonist, is not indicated for alcohol deaddiction maintenance. Opioid receptor antagonist is indicated for this condition. Drugs approved for the maintenance therapy and to prevent relapse : • Naltrexone : It is an orally active opioid receptor antagonist. • Acamprosate: An NMDA receptor antagonist with modest GABA-A receptor agonistic activity. • Disulfiram: A deterrent drug that works by inhibiting aldehyde dehydrogenase enzyme.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Tafenoquine is used in which of the following conditions?

options.d: Treatment of malaria in children <2 years

mcqs.explanation: Tafenoquine is used in the radical cure of Plasmodium vivax . Total eradication of plasmodium species which includes clinical curative and hypnozoites phase are called radical cure. Primaquine and tafenoquine (derivative of primaquine) have very high activity against the latent tissue forms (hypnozoites ) of the species . It is primarily used for the chemoprophylaxis and radical cure of P. vivax and P. ovale infections .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient diagnosed with tuberculosis is undergoing treatment with streptomycin . Which of the following is the primary intracellular site of action of this drug?
mcqs.explanation: Streptomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic and the primary intracellular site of action of aminoglycosides is the 30S ribosomal subunit . Mechanism of action of aminoglycosides : • Aminoglycosides are transported actively across the cell membrane into the cytoplasm (oxygen -dependent process ) • Binding of aminoglycosides to 30S ribosomes cause misreading of mRNA template and result in incorporation of incorrect amino acids in the growing polypeptide chain • The resulting aberrant proteins may be inserted into the cell membrane leading to altered permeability of the cell membrane of bacteria causing bacterial death (bactericidal )

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is a serious adverse effect you would consider as a possibility in a patient receiving clindamycin?
mcqs.explanation: Clindamycin use is to be limited because of the risk of pseudomembranous colitis . Pseudomembranous colitis is a lethal syndrome caused by Clostridium difficile due to alteration in normal intestinal microbiota. It is characterized by fever, watery diarrhea and increased peripheral white blood cell count. Metronidazole and oral vancomycin are used in the treatment of this condition. Drugs causing pseudomembranous colitis are: • Penicillins • Clindamycin • Rifaximin469 • Tetracycline (rare side effect ) • Erythromycin

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is false about penicillins ?

options.b: Benzathine penicillin is short acting penicillin
options.c: Cloxacillin is beta lactamase and acid resistant
options.d: Ampicillin is not resistant to beta lactamases

mcqs.explanation: Benzathine penicillin G and procaine penicillin G are repository preparations of penicillin G and are long-acting.495 They are given as deep I.M. injection. Benzathine penicillin has the longest half-life and is administered every 2-4 weeks . Penicillin V is an acid-resistant penicillin preparation that is administered orally. Ampicillin has an extended spectrum but is not resistant to beta -lactamases . Penicillinase -resistant penicillins are: • Cloxacillin • Dicloxacillin • Flucloxacillin • Methicillin • Nafcillin

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient allergic to penicillin requires antibiotic therapy . Which of the following can you safely prescribe?
mcqs.explanation: Aztreonam can be safely given to a patient with a history of allergy to penicillin . It is a monobactam group of \035-Lactam antibiotics resistant to narrow -spectrum beta -lactamase produced by bacteria. It lacks cross-sensitivity with the other beta -lactams, except for ceftazidime . It has activity only against gram-negative bacteria. It has no activity against gram-positive bacteria and anaerobes.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A 4-month-old boy was brought to the ER with recurrent seizures . His mother informs you that he is receiving isoniazid prophylaxis as she was diagnosed with TB during pregnancy. ABG revealed a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. What would be the mainstay of treatment ?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of isoniazid overdose for which the mainstay of treatment is intravenous pyridoxine. Isoniazid overdose results in decreased pyridoxine availability to neurons. This decreases the levels of GABA, which in turn lowers the seizure threshold . Benzodiazepines can be used to569 control seizures . Prolonged treatment with isoniazid leads to the deficiency of pyridoxine which can lead to peripheral neuropathy and other neurological manifestations like ataxia, paresthesia , and numbness. Clinical triad of isoniazid overdose: • Seizures refractory to treatment with phenytoin and barbiturates • High anion gap metabolic acidosis (HAGMA) resistant to treatment with sodium bicarbonate • Coma

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A 54-year-old man was brought to the casualty with fever, headache , focal seizures , and right hemiparesis . MRI brain showed hyperintensity in the left frontotemporal region. PCR of his CSF sample was positive for HSV DNA. What would be the drug of choice for this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The given clinical scenario and investigations are suggestive of HSV encephalitis for which the drug of choice is intravenous acyclovir. The treatment is effective only if it is started early. The clinical hallmark of HSV encephalitis is the acute onset of fever and focal neurologic signs with hemorrhagic necrosis of especially the temporal lobe . The most sensitive investigation is HSV DNA demonstration in CSF by PCR.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A 23 -year-old primiparous woman presented with features suggestive of thyrotoxicosis , at 7 weeks of gestation. Which of the following is the drug of choice for the treatment of her condition?
mcqs.explanation: The drug of choice for the treatment of thyrotoxicosis during the first trimester of pregnancy is propylthiouracil (PTU). It is because it has lower teratogenic effects than carbimazole or methimazole . Carbimazole and methimazole are associated with teratogenic effects such as: • Aplasia cutis congenita • Choanal atresia • Treacheosopageal fistula • Fetal goiter However, propylthiouracil use is limited to the first trimester due to the risk of hepatotoxicity . It is replaced with carbimazole or methimazole in the 2nd and 3rd trimesters of the pregnancy. The lowest effective antithyroid drug dose should be used throughout gestation . This is to maintain the maternal serum-free T4 level in the upper limit of the non-pregnant normal reference range. Radioiodine therapy is contraindicated during pregnancy and lactation.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A 65-year-old lady has been taking zoledronate for the treatment of osteoporosis . She is at a high risk of developing which of the following side effects ?
mcqs.explanation: Zoledronate use has been associated with acute renal failure. It is nephrotoxic. So baseline renal function and monitoring of renal function during therapy with zoledronate is recommended . Long term complications seen with bisphosphonate therapy are osteonecrosis of jaw and subtrochanteric fracture of femur.640

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Progestin dose remains constant throughout the cycle in which of the following type of combined contraceptive pills ?
mcqs.explanation: Monophasic pills contain constant amounts of progesterone and estrogen that is taken daily for 21 days, followed by a 7-day pill-free period. Biphasic and triphasic pills have variable amounts of active ingredients (especially progesterone ) that mimic the natural changes in the hormonal levels in the menstrual cycle . These pills reduce the total amount of steroids that needs to be administered .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A 33-year old lady with an obstetric score of G4P3L3 delivered a baby by cesarean section . She is at risk of developing uterine atony and the resident asks you to bring a long-acting analog of oxytocin. Which drug will you get ?
mcqs.explanation: Carbetocin is a long-acting analog of oxytocin. It is indicated for the prevention of uterine atony following caesarian section and for prevention of PPH. Option A: Desamino-oxytocin is a buccal formulation of oxytocin that is similar to oxytocin injection. Options C and D: Solifenacin and darifenacin are synthetic tertiary amine antimuscarinic agents that are indicated in overactive bladder .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient was on treatment with indomethacin for gout . You decide to add a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor to his treatment plan. Which of the following will you prescribe ?
mcqs.explanation: Febuxostat is a non-purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor that is indicated for reducing hyperuricemia in chronic gout . Both allopurinol and febuxostat can be used as first line agents but since the question mentions a non-purine inhibitor is chosen, febuxostat is the answer. Option A - Allopurinol is a purine xanthine oxidase inhibitor. Option D - Sulfinpyrazone is a uricosuric agent .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: After suffering from a myocardial infarction, a patient was started on two drugs X and Y. The drug X inhibits the COX -1 enzyme and drug Y inhibits thrombin-induced platelet aggregation . Identify the drugs.
mcqs.explanation: X- Aspirin and Y- Vorapaxar are the drugs administered to the patient . Aspirin reduces thromboxane A2 production by inhibiting the COX -1 enzyme. Vorapaxar is a competitive antagonist of PAR -1 and inhibits thrombin-induced platelet aggregation . Vorapaxar is indicated in combination with aspirin and/or clopidogrel to reduce thromboembolic events in patients with MI or peripheral vascular disease .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: Lab reports of a 45-year-old female patient , who was recently started on heparin, showed rapidly falling platelet counts. She was suspected to have heparin-induced thrombocytopenia . What is the most common presentation seen in this condition?
mcqs.explanation: The most common presentation of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is venous thrombosis. HIT is an immune complication of heparin therapy caused by IgG antibodies against the heparin-platelet factor 4 complex . This results in the activation of platelets to propagate a hypercoagulable state culminating in life -threatening thrombosis. It is characterized by thrombocytopenia (Platelet count <1,00,000 /�ML or reduced by over 50% from pre-treatment value) and clinically presents as venous thrombosis (in the form of DVT or pulmonary embolism) It occurs around 5-10 days after starting heparin. It is more common with UFH when compared to LMWH . It is also more common in women surgical patients . Arterial thrombosis (resulting in MI or stroke), as well as bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, can rarely occur.

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: An elderly asthmatic on treatment presented with fever, malaise, and lower limb sensory deficit . Significant investigations are given below . Which of the following drugs is associated with these findings?
mcqs.explanation: 797 The given scenario points towards a diagnosis of Churg-Strauss syndrome. It is an eosinophilic vasculitis associated with the use of montelukast and zafirlukast. This is a very rarely reported side effect of these drugs. These agents block the effects of the cysLTs (LTC4 , LTD4 , and LTE4 ) but they do not block the effect of LTB4 , which is a chemoattractant for eosinophils and neutrophils . This can lead to eosinophilia .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.chapter: Acid Peptic Disorders and Inflammatory Bowel Di...
mcqs.question: Which of the following can cause diarrhea?
mcqs.explanation: Magnesium salts have a laxative property and can cause diarrhoea. Aluminium salts can cause constipation by relaxing smooth muscles . The combination of aluminium and magnesium salts can neutralize each other's action, thus the combination is preferred .

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.chapter: Non Cell Cycle Specific Cytotoxic Drugs
mcqs.question: During a study on the cytotoxic effects of alkylating agents , you observe that cyclophosphamide has a higher cytotoxic effect compared to procarbazine. Which property of cyclophosphamide is the reason for this?
mcqs.explanation: Cyclophosphamide (nitrogen mustard) is a bifunctional alkylating agent and it results in cross-linking of DNA that causes a major disruption in nucleic acid function and increased cytotoxicity . Procarbazine is a monofunctional alkylating agent . Differences between bifunctional and monofunctional alkylating agents are:Bifunctional alkylating agent s Monofunctional alkylating a gents Usually transfers ethyl group to DNA resulting in cross-lin king Usually transfers a methyl gr oup resulting in simple meth ylation. No cross-linking of D NA Higher cytotoxicity because o f cross-linking results in a gre ater threat to cellular survival Higher carcinogenesis risk as simple methylation can be b ypassed by DNA polymerases resulting in permanent modi fication of DNA sequence

mcqs.subject: Pharmacology
mcqs.question: A patient diagnosed with wet age -related macular degeneration is being administered ranibizumab intravitreally. All of the following are known side effects of the drug, except _______.
mcqs.explanation: Ranibizumab is associated with a raise in IOP, not a fall. Ranibizumab is a monoclonal antibody directed against VEGF-A (vascular endothelial growth factor-A). Ranibizumab is indicated in wet age -related macular degeneration and is used intravitreally where it inhibits VEGF-A induced ocular neovascularization.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: A 7-year-old girl presents with skin lesions as shown in the image. The parents also complain of early breast development , growth acceleration , and vaginal bleeding . On genetic studies , it was found that there is a gain of function mutation of G Protein. What is the most probable diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: Among the given options , the most probable diagnosis is McCune -Albright syndrome as it is the only gain-of-function mutation of G Protein. G proteins or G protein-coupled receptor complexes can undergo a loss- or gain-of-function mutation. Some examples are given below : In McCune -Albright syndrome, a gain-of-function mutation in Gs�o is associated with the rough -bordered areas of skin pigmentation and hypercortisolism . This mutation occurs during fetal development , creating a mosaic of normal and abnormal cells .32 Receptor Type of mutati on Disease Cone opsin Loss Colour blindness Rhodopsin Loss Night blindness or retinitis pi gmentosa Endothelin recept or Loss Hirschsprung disease TSH receptor Loss Familialhypothyroidism TSH receptor Gain Familialhyperthyroidism LH receptor Gain Familial male precocious pub erty Gsprotein Gain Pituitary adenomas with acro megaly Gsprotein Gain (mosaic) McCune -Albright syndrome

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: If the membrane potential of this cell is -80mV the driving force is greatest for which ion?
mcqs.explanation: The driving force is greatest for Ca2+. Net driving force is the difference between the membrane potential and the equilibrium potential for that particular ion. Hence Em - EX . Where: Em = Actual membrane potential (mV ) = -80mV EX = Equilibrium potential for X (mV) For the respective ions: E Ca2+ = +120 ; Driving force = -80 – (120 ) = -200mV E Na+ = +60 ; Driving force= -80 – (60) =-140mV65 E K+ = -90, Driving force = -80 – (-90) =10mV E Cl-= -70, Driving force = -80 – (-70) =-10mV Thus, Ca2+ will have the largest driving force and it will move inwards or into the cell .

mcqs.question: Addition of 500 mL of hypertonic saline to the extracellular fluid leads to _______
mcqs.explanation: The images shown in the figure are called Darrow Yannet Diagrams. They depict the change in plasma osmolality and plasma volume in various conditions. Therefore, the net effect is an increase in extracellular volume (greater than the volume of fluid added ), a decrease in intracellular volume, and a rise in osmolarity in both compartments. mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: What process is responsible for the change in membrane potential that occurs between point 1 and point 3?

options.a: Movement of Na+ into the cell
options.b: Movement of Na+ out of the cell
options.c: Movement of K+ into the cell
options.d: Movement of K+ out of the cell

mcqs.explanation: The graph depicts action potential . The movement of Na+ into the cell is responsible for the change in membrane potential that occurs between point 1 and point 3. Once the membrane is depolarized to the threshold , local potential , the upstroke of the nerve action potential is caused by the opening of the Na+ channels. The entry of Na+ causes the opening of more voltage -gated Na+ channels and further depolarization, setting up a positive feedback loop . When the Na+ channels open , Na+ moves into the cell down its electrochemical gradient, driving the membrane potential toward the Na+ equilibrium potential .The process responsible for repolarization is the opening of K+. The K+ permeability becomes very high and drives the membrane potential toward the K+equilibrium potential by the flow of107 K+ out of the cell .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The membrane conductance for potassium is maximum at which of the following points in a nerve action potential ?
mcqs.explanation: The membrane conductance for potassium is maximum during repolarization (marked as point 3 in the above image). Most of the increase in K+ conductance comes after the increase in Na+ conductance around the time of repolarization.During the early portion of the action potential , the sodium conductance is 1000 times greater than potassium conductance . Therefore, far more sodium ions flow to the interior of the fiber than do potassium ions to the exterior. This causes the membrane potential to become positive at the action potential onset . When the membrane potential rises from � 90 millivolts toward zero, this voltage change causes a conformational change in the K+ channels which allows increased potassium efflux . Then, the sodium channels begin to close and the potassium channels begin to open , and potassium conductance begins to increase (and sodium conductance decreases ). The increased flow of K+ out of the cell causes membrane repolarization. The slow return of the K+ channels to the closed state explains the after-hyperpolarization followed by a return to the resting membrane potential .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Identify the ions A and B based on conductance graph of a neuron shown below :
mcqs.explanation: Channel A: Na+, Channel B: K+ Na+ channels are fast activating and are responsible for depolarization phase of action potential . K+ channels are slow activating and open for prolonged duration than the sodium channels. They are responsible for repolarization phase of action potential . Also, the postassium channels return slowly to their closed state , which is responsible for after-hyperpolarization.122 The sequence of events during the action potential occur in 7 steps as described below . 1. Resting state - Both channels are closed 2. Na+ channels open in response to depolarizing stimulus . Sodium enters into the cell . The membrane reaches threshold potential. 3. The sodium influx causes opening of more sodium channels through positive feedback mechanism. Rapid depolarization occurs. 4. Sodium conductance decreases . 5. Na+ channels close and K+ channels open . Repolarization occurs. 6. Sodium channels are reset , and are ready to respond to another depolarizing stimulus (relative refractory period). During this phase , the potassium channels remain open and slowly return to closed state causing after-hyperpolarization. 7. Both channels are closed . The membrane returns to RMP.123

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The image below shows simple muscle twitch along with the time trace, recorded in a frog gastrocnemius muscle . Calculate the minimum tetanizing frequency. (The time tracer was made with a 100Hz tuning fork).
mcqs.explanation: The tetanizing frequency of the muscle, based on the given diagram, is 20 per second . Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period . It is the frequency at which individual muscle fibres twitch that fuse and cause sustained muscle contraction, where the contraction period is the time taken from latent period to maximum force of contraction. In this case, the time tracer was taken using a 100Hz tuning fork. Which means the tracer recorded 100 waves per second . Therefore, the duration of each wave in time tracer = 0.01 seconds . In the image given in the question, between the point B (end of latent period ) to point C (maximum force of contraction), there are about 5 waves. Hence , the duration of contraction = 5 x 0.01 = 0.05 seconds . Substituting the value in the formula, we get : Tetanizing frequency = 1/0.05 sec = 100 /5 = 20/sec .Tetanization: The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches . The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways: • by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously , which is multiple \037ber summations. • by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization. When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level , the successive contractions eventually fuse together , and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous ,124 this is called tetanization. Beyond this point, a further increase in the frequency, will not result in increased force of contraction. Tetanization occurs in two ways: • Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli. • Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.125

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is the constituent of the marked area in the electron microscopic picture of muscle ?
mcqs.explanation: Alpha actinin is the constituent of the marked area. The image depicts sarcomere and the arrow points towards Z-line. Alpha actinin binds actin to Z-lines.The orderly arrangement of actin, myosin, and related proteins that produces this pattern. The area between two Z-lines is called sarcomere. The thick filaments , which are about twice the diameter of the thin filaments , are made up of myosin, which are lined to form A bands; the thin filaments are made up of actin, tropomyosin, and troponin. The array of thin filaments extends out of the A band and into the less dense staining I bands. The lighter H bands in the center of the A bands are the regions where , when the muscle is relaxed , the thin filaments do not overlap the thick filaments . The Z lines allow for anchoring of the thin filaments . Actinin, titin and desmin are additional structural proteins .Titin connects Z-lines to the M line and provides the scaffolding to the sarcomere. Desmin adds structure to Z-lines by connecting Z-line to plasma membrane.143 Note : Some sources say that even titin is a component of Z-disc so if alpha actinin is not given in the options titin is the second best answer.

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: The following graph displays which physiological law of the heart?
mcqs.explanation: The diagram displays the Length-Tension relationship for a cardiac muscle explaining the Starling law of the heart.167 In the body, the initial length of the fibers is determined by the degree of diastolic filling of the heart, and the pressure developed in the ventricle is proportional to the volume of the ventricle at the end of the filling phase (Starling law of the heart). • The developed tension increases as the diastolic volume increases until it reaches a maximum, then tends to decrease . • The decrease is due to beginning disruption of the myocardial fibers and not due to a decrease in the number of cross-bridges between actin and myosin as seen in skeletal muscle .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Given below is the demonstration of tetanization in the gastrocnemius muscle of a frog. Identify the tetanising frequency.
mcqs.explanation: Tetanizing frequency demonstrated by the muscle is 33Hz . Tetanizing frequency = 1/contraction period = 1000 /30 = 33Hz . Tetanization The features of muscle contraction can be demonstrated by eliciting single muscle twitches . The adding together of individual twitch contractions to increase the intensity of overall muscle contraction is Summation. Summation occurs in two ways: • by increasing the number of motor units contracting simultaneously , which is multiple \037ber summations. • by increasing the frequency of contraction, which is called frequency summation and can lead to tetanization. When the frequency of a contraction reaches a critical level , the successive contractions eventually fuse together , and the whole muscle contraction appears to be completely smooth and continuous , this is called tetanization. Tetanization occurs in two ways: • Complete tetanus occurs when no relaxation occurs between stimuli. • Incomplete tetanus when periods of incomplete relaxation take place between the summated stimuli.171

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following is true about the nature of the sensory receptor given below :
mcqs.explanation: The sensory receptor shown in the above image is Pacinian corpuscle . The Pacinian corpuscle is a rapidly adapting receptor and is an encapsulated receptor . When a stimulus of the same strength is continuously given to a sensory receptor , the frequency of the action potentials generated by the receptor gradually decreases . This phenomenon is known as receptor adaptation. Depending on whether the receptor stops responding to a stimulus rapidly or slowly , they are classified as rapidly adapting (phasic) or slow adapting receptors (tonic).

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Identify the type of nerve fibre in the diagram below .
mcqs.explanation: In the given figure , the fiber in yellow innervates the ends of the muscle spindle . Therefore, it is a gamma motor neuron. Many much smaller gamma motor neurons are located in the spinal cord anterior horns (shown as the yellow efferent fiber). These gamma motor neurons average 5 micrometers in diameter , which go to small, special skeletal muscle fibers called intrafusal fibers or the muscle spindle . These fibers constitute the ends of the muscle spindle , which help control basic muscle "tone." Option (b): The alpha motor neurons (shown as the blue efferent fibre) are on an average 14 micrometers in diameter. These fibers branch many times after they enter the muscle and innervate the large skeletal muscle fibers at the motor endplate . Stimulation of a single alpha nerve fiber excites269 anywhere from three to several hundred skeletal muscle fibers, which are collectively called the motor unit. Option (c): A-beta fibers are fibers for touch and pressure . Option (d): A-delta fibers are fibers for pain and temperature .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Homeostasis is called as dynamic equilibrium because ______

options.a: All variables are given equal importance
options.b: Can achieve a constancy in extreme environmental challenge
options.c: The set -point for all homeostatic variables is always fixed
options.d: Body maintains an internal balance within fluctuating limits

mcqs.explanation: Homeostasis is called dynamic equilibrium because the body maintains an internal balance within fluctuating limits. It describes the maintenance of nearly constant conditions in the internal environment despite changes in the outside world. A number of variables such as body temperature , blood sugar levels , blood pH, etc . are regulated within a range of values (homeostatic ranges) and not at fixed values. These variables are not given equal importance. There is a hierarchy of importance so that the constancy of certain variables may be altered markedly to maintain others within their normal range. For example , respiratory or metabolic compensation to maintain blood pH. The disruption of homeostasis either due to extreme environmental challenge or a breakdown of internal homeostatic mechanisms is termed as a disease .

mcqs.subject: Physiology
mcqs.question: Which of the following statements is true about the G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR)?

options.a: G proteins bind to hormones on the surface of the nucleus .
options.b: All the three subunits �o , \035, and \037 should bind to each other for G proteins to act.
options.c: G proteins act as inhibitory or excitatory because of differences in �o subunit .
options.d: G protein is bound to GTP in resting state .

mcqs.explanation: G proteins act as inhibitory or excitatory because of differences in �o subunit . G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are cell membrane receptors that span across the membrane 7 times hence called seven helix or serpentine receptors . G proteins have 3 subunits (�o ,\035 and \037). In its resting state , �o subunit is bound to GDP. Upon ligand binding to GPCR, it undergoes a conformational change that activates G protein within the cell . The �o subunit dissociates and in turn alters the activity of second messengers such as cAMP, cGMP or Ca2+. Once the ligand is unbound, the intrinsic GTPase activity of the �o subunit converts GTP to GDP. This leads to reassociation of �o with the \035-\037 subunit and termination of effector activation.28
